Authorities: Managerial accounting theory - cost-volume-profit with step-fixed costs

Choices.A: 10,000 units - the step does not apply below 15,000 units
Choices.B: 12,500 units - assuming the stepped-up $150K applies from zero
Choices.D: 20,000 units - highest-step fixed costs with lowest-margin assumptions

CommonTrapReference: Applying step-increment fixed costs before the step volume is reached
ExplanationCorrect: Cost-volume-profit theory with a step-function cost structure: breakeven = Fixed costs / Unit contribution margin. First-tier fixed costs of $120,000 divided by the $12 contribution margin ($30 price - $18 variable cost) = 10,000 units. Because 10,000 is below the 15,000-unit trigger, the +$30,000 step never activates at breakeven; verification: 10,000 x $12 = $120,000 exactly absorbs first-tier fixed costs. In business terms the launch repays its current cost tier well inside existing capacity. Exam trap: dividing the post-step $150,000 or $180,000 pool by $12 and reporting 12,500 or 15,000 units for volume the firm never needs to reach.
ExplanationWrongB: Choice B divides the post-step $150,000 tier by the $12 margin, but the +$30,000 increment is triggered only after unit 15,000; charging it from unit zero double-counts capacity the firm has not yet bought.
ExplanationWrongC: Choice C mistakes the 15,000-unit step threshold for the breakeven point; no fixed-cost pool in this problem divides by $12 to yield 15,000 units, so it is boundary anchoring rather than a computed result.
ExplanationWrongD: Choice D stacks the top-tier $180,000 of fixed costs and still lands on 20,000 units only by implying a $9 margin, mixing the highest cost tier with an unsupported lower contribution margin; that tier applies only above 25,000 units.
FormulaReference: Breakeven units = Fixed costs / Unit contribution margin
Stem: Riverton Products sells at $30 with variable cost of $18 (contribution margin $12). Fixed costs are $120,000 up to 15,000 units, stepping up by $30,000 (to $150,000) through 25,000 units and again above. What is the breakeven unit volume?

Choices.A: Molding binds - its 400-hour slack signals overload
Choices.B: Finishing binds - zero slack, while molding retains 400 idle hours

CommonTrapReference: Reading slack as overload - the binding constraint shows zero slack
ExplanationCorrect: Constraint identification via slack analysis: molding demand = (300 x 2) + (500 x 2) = 1,600 hours against 2,000 available, leaving 400 hours of slack; finishing demand = (300 x 1) + (500 x 3) = 1,800 hours against 1,800 available, leaving zero. The binding constraint is the resource with NO slack, so finishing limits total throughput. Production schedules, expediting priorities, and any expansion capital belong at finishing, not molding. Exam trap: calling the busier-sounding or higher-cost department the bottleneck instead of computing residual capacity per resource.
ExplanationWrongA: Choice A inverts the slack logic: 400 UNUSED molding hours mean molding is not fully consumed, so it cannot be the bottleneck; a binding constraint exhibits zero or negative slack, never surplus.
ExplanationWrongC: Choice C treats the two resources symmetrically, but molding ends with 400 idle hours while finishing is consumed to exactly 1,800 of 1,800 hours; that 400-hour differential makes equal binding impossible.
ExplanationWrongD: Choice D overlooks that planned demand consumes finishing capacity completely (1,800 of 1,800 hours), so a genuine constraint exists and throughput sequencing must run through finishing.
Stem: Barlow Products plans full demand: Product P - 300 units consuming 2 molding-hours and 1 finishing-hour each; Product Q - 500 units consuming 2 molding-hours and 3 finishing-hours each. Capacity: molding 2,000 hours; finishing 1,800 hours. Which resource is the binding constraint?
Topic: C.157 Binding constraint via slack computation
VerifiedChecks: Independent: molding 1,600/2,000 slack 400; finishing 1,800/1,800 slack 0 -> finishing binds

Choices.A: Process further - gross uplift is $13 per unit
Choices.B: Sell - extra cost exceeds the revenue uplift
Choices.C: SELL AT SPLIT-OFF - incremental analysis nets minus $7 after the $20 opportunity cost of displaced constraint time

CommonTrapReference: Omitting opportunity cost of constraint time in process-further decisions
ExplanationCorrect: Relevant costing under a binding constraint (theory of constraints): incremental revenue from further processing = $55 - $30 = $25 per unit; incremental cash cost = $12; opportunity cost of constraint time = 0.5 hours x $40 = $20. Net effect = $25 - $12 - $20 = -$7 per unit, so every unit processed further DESTROYS $7 of wealth; sell at split-off and leave the half-hour to whatever else earns $40 per hour. Business interpretation: when the bottleneck is loaded, attractive-looking upgrades are taxed by the displaced alternative use of scarce time. Exam trap: judging the upgrade on out-of-pocket costs alone ($13 apparent gain) and never charging the constraint.
ExplanationWrongA: Choice A stops at the $13 cash uplift ($25 added revenue less $12 processing cost) and omits the $20 opportunity charge for 0.5 hours of constraint time worth $40 per hour; through the bottleneck the upgrade destroys $7 per unit.
ExplanationWrongB: Choice B reaches the right action by faulty arithmetic: the $12 cash cost does not exceed the $25 revenue uplift, so the out-of-pocket comparison favors processing; only charging displaced constraint hours at $20 flips the decision to selling.
ExplanationWrongD: Choice D claims equivalence, yet selling nets $30 per unit while processing nets $23 after all costs, a $7 per-unit gap that compounds across every unit pushed through the constrained resource.
Stem: Joint product K can be sold at split-off for $30 per unit or processed further to sell at $55. Further processing costs $12 per unit in cash and consumes 0.5 hours of the plant binding constraint, whose displaced output earns $40 per hour. Process further or sell?
Topic: C.158 Sell-or-process through a binding constraint

CommonTrapReference: Ignoring the negative failure payoff when solving for break-even probability
ExplanationCorrect: Decision theory (Raiffa, 1968) frames the cutoff as the success probability at which the risky launch and the certain $80K alternative carry equal expected value: P x 500 + (1-P) x (-300) = 80, so 800P - 300 = 80 and P = 380/800 = 47.5%. Above 47.5%, launching adds expected value over the safe option; below it, take the certain $80K. In business terms the hurdle is steep because failure burns $300K while success earns a net $500K swing. Exam trap: treating the failure outcome as zero rather than negative $300K, which drags the true cutoff far above the naive 37.5% loss-share figure.
ExplanationWrongA: Choice A divides the certain $80K safe payoff by the $500K success payoff (80/500 = 16%), ignoring the failure branch entirely; the indifference point must weight the -$300K loss, not just the upside.
ExplanationWrongB: Choice B computes 300/(500+300) = 37.5%, the loss share of the total payoff swing; that answers a different question and drops the $80K safe alternative that actually sets the indifference standard.
ExplanationWrongC: Choice C rearranges the indifference equation as (500-80)/700 = 60%, scaling only the success side by the payoff spread; correctly, both branches enter the weighted average, giving 800P - 300 = 80 and 47.5%.
FormulaReference: Indifference probability: P x Success payoff + (1-P) x Failure payoff = Certain alternative
Stem: A launch pays $500,000 if successful and loses $300,000 if it fails; the safe alternative earns $80,000 certain. At what success probability are the two courses equally attractive?

Authorities: Managerial accounting theory - cost of prediction error

Choices.D: $0 - no contract was signed so nothing was lost

CommonTrapReference: Measuring prediction error as the estimate gap instead of forgone optimal-action value
ExplanationCorrect: Cost of prediction error (decision theory / managerial accounting): the measure is the benefit forgone versus the OPTIMAL decision, not the size of the forecasting miss. Had managers known the true $20 variable cost, they would have accepted and earned 5,000 x ($22 - $20) = $10,000 of contribution. Because they believed cost was $24, they declined, so the estimate error cost exactly $10,000. The $4 per-unit estimate gap ($24 vs $20) is diagnostic detail, not the loss metric. Exam trap: multiplying the estimate-to-actual gap by volume ($4 x 5,000 = $20,000) and reporting that as the decision cost.
ExplanationWrongB: Choice B multiplies the $4 per-unit forecasting miss ($24 estimate versus $20 truth) by all 5,000 units, measuring estimate quality instead of decision damage; prediction error is priced against the optimal action, not the estimate gap.
ExplanationWrongC: Choice C shrinks the loss to a token figure, as if only a sliver of the order were affected; the entire 5,000-unit order carried $2 of real contribution per unit that management declined, so the full margin evaporates.
ExplanationWrongD: Choice D assumes unsigned contracts create no loss, the classic sunk-thinking error; the cost of a bad prediction is the benefit forgone relative to the decision that would have been optimal, whether or not cash ever moved.
FormulaReference: Cost of prediction error = Volume x (Offer price - True unit variable cost)
Stem: Hartwell Textiles quoted a 5,000-unit special order at $22 against an ESTIMATED variable cost of $24 and declined. True variable cost was later shown to be $20. What is the cost of the prediction error?

Authorities: Decision theory - expected value of sample information (Raiffa 1968)
CommonTrapReference: Comparing against gross EVSI without netting the information purchase price
ExplanationCorrect: Expected value of sample information: gross EVSI = EV with information - EV without = $340,000 - $220,000 = $120,000. Net benefit = $120,000 - $90,000 study fee = +$30,000, so commissioning the study adds value. Decision theory (Bayesian revision, Raiffa 1968) requires netting the price of information against the decision improvement it purchases; information is an investment, not a free upgrade. Business interpretation: a $90K study that moves expected outcomes by $120K clears its hurdle with $30K to spare. Exam trap: authorizing research up to the GROSS $120,000 figure while ignoring what the study itself costs.
ExplanationWrongA: Choice A quotes the gross expected value WITH sample information ($340,000) as if it were the net benefit, ignoring both the $220,000 baseline and the $90,000 fee that must be netted out.
ExplanationWrongC: Choice C reports the gross value of information ($340,000 - $220,000 = $120,000) before deducting the study cost, overstating the case for commissioning by exactly the $90,000 fee.
ExplanationWrongD: Choice D treats the $90,000 price tag as the whole answer, implying information can never pay; the fee must be compared with the $120,000 of decision improvement it enables, leaving +$30,000 on the table.
FormulaReference: Net EVSI = (EV with information - EV without) - Information cost
Stem: Management computes EV WITH the proposed market study at $340,000, EV WITHOUT it at $220,000; the study costs $90,000. Should the study be commissioned, and what is its net benefit?
Topic: C.161 Net value of sample information after study cost

Choices.A: 25.0% - the margin on price restated as markup

CommonTrapReference: Quoting margin-on-price when markup-on-variable-cost is requested
ExplanationCorrect: Optimal pricing via the Lerner condition: profit maximization requires (P - VC)/P = 1/|Ed|. With Ed = -4, the margin on price is 25%, so P = VC/0.75 and the markup ON VARIABLE COST = (P - VC)/VC = 0.25/0.75 = 33.3%, equivalently 1/(|Ed| - 1) = 1/3. Worked example: for a product with $60 variable cost, price = $60/0.75 = $80, a $20 markup on $60. Business meaning: the more elastic the demand, the thinner the sustainable markup. Exam trap: answering with the 25% margin-on-price when the question asks for markup-on-cost - the two differ by their denominator.
ExplanationWrongA: Choice A restates the Lerner margin on price ((P - VC)/P = 1/4 = 25%) as if it were a markup on variable cost; converting a 25% margin to a cost basis gives 0.25/0.75 = 33.3%, which is what was asked.
ExplanationWrongB: Choice B comes from adding the elasticity to the denominator (1/(4+1) = 20%), a sign-and-arithmetic slip; the correct conversion subtracts one: 1/(4-1) = 33.3%.
ExplanationWrongD: Choice D reads the elasticity magnitude straight as a percentage (4 mapped to 400%), conflating an elasticity index with a cost-plus markup; elasticities measure responsiveness, not pricing multiples.
Stem: Market research measures Apex's thermostat demand elasticity at minus 4. What markup ON VARIABLE COST moves pricing toward the contribution-maximizing point?
Topic: C.162 Optimal markup from demand elasticity

Authorities: Managerial accounting theory - dual-rate transfer pricing
CommonTrapReference: Reporting one division's gross transfer instead of the centrally absorbed wedge
ExplanationCorrect: Dual-rate transfer pricing: the seller books the market price ($140 per unit) while the buyer is charged variable cost ($85 per unit); the $55 per-unit divergence on all 8,000 units is absorbed by corporate: ($140 - $85) x 8,000 = $440,000. Headquarters deliberately carries this wedge so the seller stays motivated at full market economics while the buyer sees marginal-cost economics for sourcing decisions. Exam trap: reporting either division's gross transfer ($680,000 buyer side or $1,120,000 seller side), or the bare $55 unit wedge, instead of the aggregate central absorption.
ExplanationWrongA: Choice A stops at the $55 per-unit wedge ($140 market credit less $85 variable charge) and never scales it; corporate absorption is a dollar TOTAL: $55 x 8,000 units.
ExplanationWrongB: Choice B reports the buyer side of the ledger ($85 x 8,000 = $680,000), one division's transfer bill, not the central spread absorbed between the two posted prices.
ExplanationWrongC: Choice C reports the seller side ($140 x 8,000 = $1,120,000), the market-basis credit booked by the selling division, mistaking a single division's gross transfer for the corporate plug.
FormulaReference: Corporate absorption = (Market transfer price - Variable cost) x Units transferred
Stem: Marlin's Engine Division transfers 8,000 units to Assembly: Engine records revenue at the $140 market price while Assembly is charged the $85 variable cost; corporate absorbs the difference. How much does CORPORATE absorb for the period?
